drills.title: Break-even move from implied vol
drills.question: An index option trades at 25% implied vol. What daily move (%) does a delta-hedged long position need to break even? What weekly move if you re-hedge weekly?
common_mistakes: Dividing by 252 instead of sqrt(252)
Using 365 calendar days for a trading-day move
Thinking the move must be in one direction
drills.intuition: The option's theta is the rent for gamma. It is paid back when the squared move equals implied variance per period, whatever the sign.
drills.takeaway: Translate every implied vol into a daily move and compare it with the moves you actually see.

drills.title: Put-call parity check
drills.question: Stock 200, no dividends. Three-month European options struck at 190: call 15.40, put 3.10. r = 5% continuous. What does parity say C - P should be, and what is the gap (quoted C - P minus parity)? Each option has a 0.20 bid-ask spread. Is there an arbitrage?
drills.solution: Parity: C - P = S - K e^{-rT} = 200 - 190 e^{-0.0125} = 200 - 187.640 = 12.360. Quoted C - P = 12.30. Gap = -0.06. Crossing two 0.20 spreads costs about 0.20 (half-spread on each of two legs), more than the gap. No arbitrage.
common_mistakes: Discounting the strike with simple interest
Comparing the gap with mid prices only, ignoring spreads
Forgetting the cost of shorting the stock leg
drills.intuition: Parity is a static replication: call minus put is a forward. It holds for any volatility.
drills.takeaway: Small parity gaps are usually costs, dividends or borrow fees, not arbitrage.

drills.title: Hedged long option in a quiet market
drills.question: You bought 20,000 units of an at-the-money option at 18% implied vol and delta-hedged daily. Realized vol came in at 14%. Vega is 0.20 per vol point per unit. (a) Approximate the P&L. (b) Your colleague says the loss means the market 'went the wrong way'. Respond.

rubric: States that the hedged P&L depends on realized versus implied variance, not on direction
Notes the vega approximation ignores path dependency: P&L is gamma-weighted, so it depends on where the moves occurred relative to the strike
Mentions discrete hedging noise and transaction costs as further sources of difference

drills.solution: P&L ~ vega x (sigma_r - sigma_i) x units = 0.20 x (14 - 18) x 20,000 = -$16,000. Direction is irrelevant to a delta-hedged position; the loss came from paying theta at an 18% rate while gamma earned at about 14%.
common_mistakes: Attributing a delta-hedged loss to direction
Using vol differences in decimals with vega quoted per vol point
Treating the approximation as exact
drills.intuition: A hedged option is a swap of realized variance for implied variance, weighted by gamma.
drills.takeaway: Before buying options for a view, say where and when you expect realized vol to exceed implied.

drills.title: Choosing a cap strike under a DSCR test
drills.question: A $30m two-year floating loan at SOFR + 3.25% on a property with NOI $3.0m. The lender requires DSCR >= 1.25x at the cap strike. Flat forward 4.00%, normal vol 1.10%, quarterly caplets, first period excluded (cap_premium convention). (a) Maximum strike. (b) DSCR at a 4.50% strike. (c) Premium of the 4.50% cap. (d) Premium of the 5.00% cap. Which strike do you buy?

rubric: Rejects the 5.00% strike because DSCR at the strike (1.21x) fails the covenant, however cheap it is
Recognizes the covenant sets the maximum strike, and tests DSCR at the strike on stressed NOI before settling at 4.50%
Notes the premium must be budgeted at a dealer quote and that a cap shorter than the loan creates replacement risk

common_mistakes: Buying the cheapest strike without checking the covenant
Sizing DSCR at today's SOFR rather than the strike
Ignoring that both strikes are out of the money and therefore vega-heavy
drills.intuition: The cap's strike is chosen by cash flow; its price by the forward and the vol.
drills.takeaway: Covenant first, cash-flow stress second, price third.

drills.title: Futures hedge and margin buffer
drills.question: Hedge $25m of REIT shares with index futures at 5,000 ($50 multiplier). Correlation 0.80, vols 20% (REITs) and 16% (futures). (a) Hedge ratio. (b) Contracts. (c) Hedge effectiveness. (d) Variation margin owed on a 5% index rally.
common_mistakes: Setting the hedge ratio to 1 by assumption rather than from rho and vols
Forgetting the $50 multiplier
Assuming the shares' offsetting gain can fund the margin
drills.intuition: A futures hedge swaps price risk for basis and liquidity risk.
drills.takeaway: Size the cash buffer to a stress move in the hedge, not to the expected move.

drills.title: Swap breakage on an early sale
drills.question: A borrower pays fixed 4.25% on a $20m swap with two annual payments left (accrual 1.0, on a reset date). Annually compounded zero rates are now 3.25% (1y) and 3.40% (2y). The property is being sold and the loan repaid. (a) Annuity factor. (b) Current par swap rate. (c) Termination value to the borrower (pay-fixed). Who pays whom?
common_mistakes: Assuming the swap terminates for free with the loan
Getting the sign backwards: pay-fixed loses when rates fall
Using the original swap rate as the discount rate
drills.intuition: A swap is a fixed-rate loan's prepayment penalty in disguise: it crystallizes when you exit after rates fall.
drills.takeaway: When the exit date is uncertain, compare the swap's breakage distribution with a cap's premium.

drills.title: The 'zero-cost' collar on a hotel loan

inputs.offered_structure: zero-cost collar: cap at 5.00%, floor at 3.25%

drills.question: A lender's affiliate offers the sponsor of a hotel with a $40m three-year floating loan a 'zero-cost collar': a cap at 5.00% paid for by selling a floor at 3.25%. The sponsor plans to sell in 12–36 months. No vol quotes by strike, no termination terms and no credit-support terms are provided. Your deal team wants you to sign today to 'lock in free protection'. What do you do?

rubric: Recommends not signing today (abstain) until strike-specific vol quotes, termination/assignment terms and credit-support terms are received; the cheapest correct answer is to wait or buy a plain cap

Explains that a collar is long a cap and short a floor, so 'zero cost' means the sponsor sells floor value equal to the cap premium; if rates fall, the floor creates a mark-to-market liability that crystallizes on an early sale, like swap breakage
Notes that with an uncertain exit (12–36 months) the floor liability is most likely to be owed when rates have fallen in a downturn, when a sale may be forced
Identifies that pricing cannot be checked without vol quotes by strike (skew matters for both legs) and that a lender affiliate as counterparty may hold the dealer spread invisibly
States what would change the answer: competitive quotes from at least two dealers, a termination formula, assignability to a buyer, and an exit date that is near-certain

drills.solution: Abstain for now. 'Zero cost' is a statement about the upfront premium, not about value or risk: the sponsor is short a 3.25% floor. On an early sale after rates fall below 3.25%, the sponsor owes the floor's market value. Without strike-specific vol quotes the sponsor cannot check whether the floor sold is worth more than the cap bought (the hidden fee). Request quotes and terms, compare with a plain 5.00% cap bought for cash, and decide then.
common_mistakes: Treating zero upfront cost as zero cost
Ignoring the floor's breakage on an early exit
Accepting a single quote from an affiliated counterparty
drills.intuition: Every 'free' hedge is paid for by an option you sold.
drills.takeaway: Name each option you are long and short before signing a hedge, and price the one you sold.
